title: The Arabic Feature Against Its Closest Neuron
takeaway: Plotted against the single neuron whose behaviour is closest to it, the Arabic script feature separates Arabic contexts and Arabic output tokens along its own axis, while the neuron's axis does not separate them at all. The paper reads this as evidence that dictionary learning did not simply rediscover an already-clean neuron: correlations of 0.09 on activations and 0.21 on logit weights are non-zero but slight.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots, both setting the [[arabic-script-feature]] A/1/3450 against one MLP neuron, A/neurons/489.

That neuron is not picked at random. It is the [[most-correlated-neuron]]: the one whose activations track the feature's most closely over roughly 40 million dataset examples. So it is the best single-neuron stand-in for this feature that exists in the model.

In the left panel each point is a token in the data. Its horizontal position is the neuron's activation there; its vertical position is the feature's. In the right panel each point is a vocabulary token, positioned by the neuron's [[logit-weight]] on it horizontally and the feature's vertically — how much each one pushes that token's next-token logit up or down when it fires.

### How to read it

Colour carries the [[arabic-script-proxy]]'s verdict on the token: red for Arabic script, blue for everything else, with the paler blues marking weaker proxy scores.

Both axes have a separate lane for exactly zero, with `>0` marking where the continuous range starts. Most tokens sit in that zero lane, which is what the "most probability mass is at zero" note points at.

The bars along the left and bottom edges are stacked marginal histograms ([[feature-neuron-scatter-plots]]). Each bar is normalised, so its colour split shows the composition at that activation level, not a count.

### What it shows

Read the y-marginals downward. Above a feature activation of about 5 the bar is solid red, and the red share shrinks as the activation falls toward zero. A high feature value implies an Arabic context — that is [[activation-specificity]]. The right panel repeats it: above a feature logit weight of roughly 0.4 the bar turns red, and the ringed cluster near 0.5–0.6 is labelled "Arabic Token Logits".

Now read the x-marginals across. Red is a thin sliver at the base at every neuron value, and stays about that thin the whole way. The neuron's value barely narrows down the context, because it responds to a mixture of non-English languages rather than to Arabic alone.

The paper rings the tilted blue cloud at the origin "Interference Weights?" — its guess that this near-zero mass is cross-talk forced by [[superposition]], not deliberate behaviour ([[weight-interference]]).

terms.definition: The paper's identifier for the feature under study: model A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 3450. It is the Arabic script feature, the lead case study of Section 3.
Neuron 489 of the MLP in transformer A — an actual hidden unit of the model, not a learned dictionary feature. It is the neuron whose activations correlate most strongly with A/1/3450's.

terms.term: A / B (the first slot in the identifier)
terms.definition: Which of the two identically-trained one-layer transformers the object comes from; they differ only in initialisation seed. Everything in this figure is from transformer A.
Writing "neurons" where a run index would go signals that the identifier names a transformer MLP neuron rather than an autoencoder feature, so the two can be compared without ambiguity.
The left panel compares when the feature fires against when the neuron fires, token by token over the dataset.
The right panel compares what the feature does to the output distribution against what the neuron does, token by token over the vocabulary.
The subtitle of each panel, giving the Pearson correlation of the two quantities plotted in that panel. It is the single number summarising how much the neuron resembles the feature.

terms.term: Feature Activaitons (Run A) — y-axis, left panel
terms.definition: The activation of A/1/3450 on a token. The typo and the "Run A" wording are the plotting template's; the panel title makes clear this axis is the feature.

terms.term: Feature Activations (Run B) — x-axis, left panel
terms.definition: Despite the "Run B" label carried over from the template used for cross-model comparisons, the panel title and the surrounding text identify this axis as the activation of neuron A/neurons/489.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A) — y-axis, right panel
terms.definition: The feature's logit weight on a vocabulary token: how much that token's next-token logit moves when A/1/3450 is active, through the linear path from the feature direction to the unembedding.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A Neuron) — x-axis, right panel
terms.definition: The same quantity computed for neuron 489 instead of the feature. This label states explicitly that the horizontal axis belongs to the neuron.

A vector with one entry per vocabulary token, obtained by pushing the feature (or neuron) direction through the MLP output weights, a linearised layer norm, and the unembedding. Each entry says how much firing raises or lowers that token's logit.

Because softmax is shift-invariant, logit weights have no absolute zero; the paper shifts each feature's weight vector so its median is zero. This is why the blue bulk in the right panel sits centred on the origin.

Tokens the Arabic script proxy scores as Arabic script. In the left panel that means the token appears in an Arabic-script context; in the right panel it means the vocabulary token is an Arabic-script token.

terms.term: Blue points and blue bars (dark to pale)
terms.definition: Tokens the proxy does not score as Arabic. The shades correspond to bands of the proxy's likelihood-ratio score, stacked from least Arabic-like to most.
A per-token score $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$ built from the Arabic Unicode blocks, used as a stand-in for "is this Arabic script?" so feature activations can be broken down by context.

The stacked, normalised histogram along the left edge of a panel: for each level of the feature's value, the colour split of the tokens at that level. It answers "given this feature value, what kind of token is this?".
The stacked, normalised histogram along the bottom edge: for each level of the neuron's value, the colour split of the tokens at that level. It answers the same question for the neuron.
The property that the variable being high implies the hypothesised context is present. Here the feature's axis has it and the neuron's axis does not — that asymmetry is the whole point of the figure.
A break in both axes: the value exactly zero gets its own narrow lane, and the continuous positive range begins at this marker. Without the break, the enormous zero bin would swamp the plot.

terms.term: 0 (the separate lane and the dot at the corner)
terms.definition: The bin holding tokens where the feature, the neuron, or both are exactly off. The narrow strips between the marginals and the scatter hold the points with one coordinate at zero.
An annotation with a dotted leader pointing at the origin bin, noting that the overwhelming majority of tokens sit there because both the feature and the neuron are inactive almost all the time.

A hand-drawn ring around the small cluster of Arabic-script vocabulary tokens sitting high on the feature's logit-weight axis. This is the far-right second mode of the feature's logit weight distribution seen edge-on.

A hand-drawn ring around the large near-zero cloud, with a question mark. The paper's tentative reading is that this mass is unwanted cross-talk imposed by superposition rather than anything the model uses.

Because feature directions in superposition cannot all be orthogonal, activating one feature slightly activates and slightly moves the logits of others. That leakage is what "interference weights" would be.

The hypothesis that a network encodes more features than it has neurons, giving each feature its own linear combination of neurons. It is why a feature like this one need not line up with any single neuron.

terms.term: Mixture of non-English languages (the neuron's actual role)
terms.definition: The paper's description of what neuron 489 responds to. It offers this as a sensible superposition strategy, since languages are close to mutually exclusive and so are cheap to pack together.

terms.term: The feature is not a neuron
terms.definition: The check this figure serves: confirming that dictionary learning found something the neuron basis does not already expose, rather than handing back a conveniently clean neuron under a new name.
Reference lines marking zero logit weight on each axis, so the reader can see that the blue bulk is centred on no-effect and the red cluster is not.
Annotation drawn over the scatter by the authors to pick out two point populations. They are not fitted contours and carry no statistical claim.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and neuron 489's activations across the dataset. It is the headline number of the left panel: the most feature-like neuron in the model still barely tracks the feature.

Pearson correlation between the feature's logit weight vector and the neuron's, over the vocabulary. Slightly larger than the activation correlation — the tilt of the blue cloud — but the paper calls the similarity minimal.
The index of the feature within dictionary learning run A/1. It carries no meaning beyond identifying the feature.
The index of the neuron within transformer A's MLP, which has 512 neurons. It was selected by correlation search, not by position.
The dictionary learning run the feature comes from. Runs A/0 through A/5 share a fixed L1 coefficient and increase in dictionary size, so the run index fixes how many features were learned.
The number of dataset examples over which the paper searched for the neuron most correlated with the feature. A large sweep is needed because the feature fires on a very small fraction of tokens.
The range of activation values for the feature and the neuron. Both are post-ReLU, so neither goes below zero, and the axes are broken so exact zero sits in its own lane.
The level above which the paper reports the feature is 98% specific to Arabic script. In the left y-marginal this is roughly where the bar becomes solid red with no blue left.
Where the bottom histogram flattens into a single pale band. Beyond this point so few tokens fall in each bin that the composition stops varying.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic script, from the specificity section. It is the base rate, and it is why red is a thin sliver in every x-marginal bin: at a typical neuron activation the composition is close to the background distribution.
The share of tokens on which the feature is active that are Arabic script. Against a 0.13% base rate, this is what "specific" means for this feature.

The Arabic share when the feature is barely active versus when its activation is above 5. The gap between them is exactly the gradient you see running up the left y-marginal, from mostly blue at the bottom to solid red at the top.
The plotted range of logit weights. Values are median-centred per feature, so zero means no effect on that token's logit and the scale is relative, not absolute.
Roughly where the right panel's y-marginal flips from almost entirely blue to majority red. Above this the tokens the feature promotes are predominantly Arabic script.

The band holding the ringed "Arabic Token Logits" cluster. These are the vocabulary tokens whose probability the feature raises most, and they sit spread across the neuron's axis, showing the neuron does not single them out.

From the same section: searching every neuron's top 20 dataset examples for Arabic script turned up one neuron with a single Arabic example; eighteen of its remaining examples were English and one Cyrillic. This is the separate check that no neuron is an Arabic neuron.

numbers.value: 3 (largest coefficients, all negative) and 27 (coefficients at least 0.1 in magnitude)
numbers.meaning: The feature's decomposition in the neuron basis, reported just before this figure. The feature is spread over dozens of neurons, and its three strongest components point the wrong way, which is what motivated looking at the correlated neuron instead.
The number of ReLU neurons in the one-layer transformer's MLP, the pool from which neuron 489 was selected.
